big_case.notes: Significant Solicitor General emergency application resulting in a 6-page published per curiam opinion (26A560) staying a district court injunction against over 300 miles of border-barrier construction in the Big Bend Sector and clarifying that major-questions-doctrine challenges are statutory rather than constitutional claims under Dalton v. Specter and IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(A).

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt, pp. 5-6) grants the application for stay pending the timely filing and disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari and declines summary reversal, noting that Respondents' alternative constitutional claims were not reached by the district court.
central_claims.claim: The Court will grant the application for a stay of the October 2, 2026 preliminary injunction pending the filing and disposition of a timely petition for a writ of certiorari, while declining the alternative request for certiorari before judgment and summary reversal.

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt, pp. 2-4) holds that § 102(c)(2)(A) bars non-constitutional claims and relies on Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462, 472-474 (1994), and West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 723-724 (2022), to conclude that the district court lacked jurisdiction over the major-questions claim.
central_claims.claim: Under IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(A), Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462, 472 (1994), and West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 721, 723 (2022), a major-questions challenge is a statutory interpretation claim rather than a constitutional claim, so the district court lacked jurisdiction.

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt, pp. 4-5) holds that even assuming jurisdiction, the major-questions claim fails on the merits under § 102(a) and § 102(c)(1), and rejects reading 'comparatively' into 'areas of high illegal entry' (citing In re Border Infrastructure Environmental Litigation, 915 F.3d 1213, 1224 (9th Cir. 2019), and the 89,000 apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector from FY2021-FY2025).
central_claims.claim: Even assuming the district court had jurisdiction, the major-questions claim fails on the merits because IIRIRA § 102(a), (b), and (c)(1) expressly authorize the Secretary in his sole discretion to waive all legal requirements for border barrier construction, and the district court erred by reading a comparative-apprehensions requirement into 'areas of high illegal entry' (citing In re Border Infrastructure, 915 F.3d at 1224).

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt, pp. 5-6) cites Trump v. CASA, Inc., 606 U.S. 831, 861 (2025), Trump v. Sierra Club, 588 U.S. 930 (2019), and TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153, 194 (1978), for these exact propositions.
central_claims.claim: The government suffers irreparable harm when enjoined from carrying out its statutory authority (citing Trump v. CASA, Inc., 606 U.S. 831, 861 (2025)), and under Trump v. Sierra Club, 588 U.S. 930 (2019), and TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153, 194 (1978), Congress subordinated the waived environmental and aesthetic interests to expeditious barrier construction.

central_claims.basis: While the Court did issue a per curiam opinion (01-per-curiam.txt), no Justice noted a dissent.
central_claims.claim: The Court will likely issue either an unsigned order or a brief per curiam opinion, with Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson likely to note dissents.
